title: The Invisible Scoreboard: 9 Rules To Navigate Office Politics
author: The Good Boss
summary: The Good Boss makes the case that office politics is not an optional game — every organization runs an invisible scoreboard that tracks who gets listened to, who gets credit, who is trusted with important work, and who is perceived as a threat. Leaders who refuse to engage with politics do not escape it; they simply play it without knowing the rules or tracking the score. The nine rules laid out are less about manipulation and more about intentional social intelligence: understanding who holds informal power, building alliances before you need them, managing your reputation proactively, and reading the organizational landscape as a system rather than a collection of individuals. The article treats political skill as a form of social competence rather than cynical maneuvering, arguing that leaders who are politically skilled are more effective — not less ethical — because they understand the human dynamics through which decisions actually get made. The final rule returns to character: the most durable political asset is a reputation for doing what you say, protecting your people, and making others look good.
points: Refusing to engage with office politics does not exempt you from it — it means you are being scored without knowing the rules, which is the worst possible position in any competitive environment.

The invisible scoreboard tracks informal social capital: who gets listened to in unstructured settings, who is included in early conversations, and whose judgment is trusted when decisions are ambiguous — all independent of formal organizational authority.

Political intelligence is a form of social literacy: understanding who influences whom, where coalitions form, and what each stakeholder actually wants (versus what they say they want) is essential information for effective leadership.

Building alliances before you need them is the political equivalent of building savings before a crisis — reciprocity developed under low-stakes conditions is far more reliable than favors requested in moments of need.

The deepest political asset is character: leaders who protect their people, follow through on commitments, and make others look good accumulate social capital that outlasts the inevitable power shifts in any organization.
quotes: There’s a “scoreboard” in every organization. Not the Jira dashboards or the AI Tokens dashboards that you might be thinking.
